content: Pediatrics, also spelled paediatrics, is a specialized branch of medicine that focuses on the medical care of infants, children, and adolescents. The upper age limit for pediatric care varies by country, ranging from 14 to 21 years. A medical professional who specializes in this field is referred to as a pediatrician (or paediatrician). Pediatricians may hold either a DO (Doctor of Osteopathy) or an MD (Doctor of Medicine) degree. The term pediatrics originates from the Greek words pais (child) and iatros (doctor or healer), meaning healer of children. Differences Between Adult and Pediatric Medicine Pediatrics differs significantly from adult medicine in various aspects. The physiological differences between a child and an adult are not merely a matter of size but also involve developmental and maturational changes. For instance, the smaller body of an infant or neonate functions differently from that of an adult. Pediatricians often address congenital defects, genetic variations, and other conditions that are less commonly encountered in adult medicine. Certain diseases, such as sickle cell anemia and cystic fibrosis, are more frequently managed by pediatricians because advancements in medical care have only recently allowed many of these patients to survive into adulthood. Additionally, pediatricians are primarily responsible for managing infectious diseases and immunizations in children. Treating a child is not equivalent to treating a miniature adult. Childhood is a period of rapid growth, development, and maturation of various organ systems. Pediatricians undergo extensive training to distinguish between normal developmental variations and pathological conditions. Another key difference is that children are minors and, in most jurisdictions, cannot make medical decisions for themselves. Issues such as guardianship, privacy, legal responsibility, and informed consent must be carefully considered in every pediatric procedure. Pediatricians often find themselves treating not only the child but also addressing the concerns of the parents and, at times, the entire family. Adolescents occupy a unique legal category, with limited rights to make their own healthcare decisions, which vary by region and legal context. History of Pediatrics The origins of pediatrics as a distinct medical field can be traced back to the 10th century when the Persian physician Rhazes (Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi) authored The Diseases of Children, the first book dedicated to pediatric medicine. Rhazes is often regarded as the father of pediatrics. His teacher, Ali ibn Sahl Rabban al-Tabari, was also a pioneer in child development, which he discussed in his earlier work, Firdous al-Hikmah. In the Western world, the first pediatric text was The Book of Children, written around 1530 by Thomas Phaer, who was influenced by the works of Rhazes and Avicenna. Pediatrics as a separate medical specialty in the West began to emerge in the 19th century. The Hospital for Sick Children in Great Ormond Street, London, founded in 1852, is one of the oldest children's hospitals in the English-speaking world. Abraham Jacobi, a German physician who emigrated to the United States, is often considered the father of American pediatrics. Training of Pediatricians The training required to become a pediatrician varies widely across the globe. Like other physicians, pediatricians begin their education with an entry-level medical degree, which is typically a tertiary-level course offered by a university-affiliated medical school. Depending on the country and institution, this may be an undergraduate-entry program lasting five to six years or a graduate-entry program lasting four to five years, following a prior university degree (often in the sciences). Medical graduates earn a degree specific to their country and institution, qualifying them for licensure or registration under national laws. In some cases, additional requirements such as internships or conditional registration may apply. Pediatricians must then undergo further specialized training in their chosen field, which can take three to six or more years, depending on the jurisdiction and level of specialization. Training for primary care pediatricians is generally shorter than for hospital-based specialists. In some countries, pediatric specialization begins immediately after completing entry-level medical training, while in others, junior doctors must first complete generalist training before pursuing a pediatric specialty. Specialist training is often overseen by pediatric organizations rather than universities, with varying degrees of government involvement depending on the country. Pediatrician vs. Paediatrician The spelling of pediatrician (American English) versus paediatrician (British English) reflects a slight semantic difference. In the United States, a pediatrician is typically a primary care physician specializing in children, similar to a general practitioner. In Germany, a kinderarzt serves a similar role. In the Commonwealth and many other parts of the world, a paediatrician is usually a specialist physician who sees patients referred by general practitioners or those urgently admitted to hospitals. In this context, a paediatrician could be described as an internist who has subspecialized in child health, often undergoing more extensive post-graduate training than a primary care pediatrician. Subspecialists in Pediatrics Pediatricians may pursue additional training in subspecialties. Practicing a pediatric subspecialty often involves managing diseases that are common in children but rare in adults, such as bronchiolitis or rotavirus infections. Conversely, conditions frequently seen in adults, such as coronary artery disease or deep vein thrombosis, are uncommon in children. For example, pediatric cardiologists focus on congenital heart defects, while pediatric oncologists treat cancers like leukemia, lymphomas, and sarcomas, which are more prevalent in children than adults. Every adult medical specialty has a pediatric counterpart, except for geriatrics. Adolescent medicine is a growing subspecialty, addressing conditions that overlap with those seen in older adults. Neonatology, the care of newborns, is a unique subspecialty within pediatrics. Pediatric Organizations Most pediatricians are members of national or regional professional organizations. Examples include the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Canadian Paediatric Society, the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, and the Indian Academy of Pediatrics. In Australia and New Zealand, pediatricians are fellows of the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, which encompasses both adult and pediatric medicine. In the United Kingdom, pediatricians were historically members or fellows of the Royal College of Physicians until the establishment of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health in 1996. Social Role of Pediatricians Pediatricians, like other physicians, are traditionally regarded as members of a learned profession due to their extensive training and the ethical and legal responsibilities of their work. They often enjoy high social status, along with expectations of stable income and job security. However, medical practitioners frequently work long, inflexible hours, including shifts at unsociable times. Neonatologists and hospital-based pediatricians are often on call for high-risk births, such as Caesarean sections, or for the care of critically ill newborns. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, general pediatricians earned an average salary of $141,440 in 2006.
